deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of §§4–5 of Riemann's published memoir 'Ein Beitrag zu den Untersuchungen über die Bewegung eines gleichartigen flüssigen Ellipsoides' (Abh. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 9, 1861). In that memoir the motion of a homogeneous self-gravitating liquid ellipsoid with semi-axes a, b, c is described by two sets of angular-velocity components: (u, v, w) for the rotation of the principal-axis frame and (u', v', w') for the internal, vortical part of the motion.

(A) End of the analysis of figures of fixed shape and orientation-independent motion. The equations (1) leave several alternatives:
- the earlier assumption (rotation about a principal axis only);
- u' = v' = 0 (or similar), which is not essentially different;
- u = v = w = 0.
Under u = v = w = 0 the differential equations (1) give v'w' = w'u' = u'v' = 0, so two of u', v', w' must vanish.
Conclusion (Riemann's theorem): a liquid ellipsoid can keep its shape during the motion only if the normal to the invariable plane (the angular-momentum vector) and the instantaneous rotation axis lie in one principal plane. The motion is then a superposition of two parts:
- an internal motion in which the particles describe similar, parallel ellipses lying in planes perpendicular to that principal plane;
- a rigid rotation of the whole about an axis lying in that principal plane.
This is the classification of the 'Riemann ellipsoids' (Chandrasekhar's types S, I, II, III).

(B) Back to the case u, u', v, v' = 0, i.e. rotation and vorticity both about the principal axis c. (The transcription lists u, u', v, v', w, w' as permanently zero; logically only the u and v components vanish here.) Riemann observes that the equations (1) for a(t), b(t), c(t) are those of a unit mass point (a, b, c) moving on the surface abc = const in a potential
 G = τ²/(a−b)² + τ'²/(a+b)² − 2εK.
Here:
- τ and τ' are constants built from the conserved angular momentum and circulation;
- ε is proportional to the gravitational constant times density;
- K = ∫_0^∞ ds/√((a²+s)(b²+s)(c²+s)) up to a constant factor (my identification), the gravitational self-energy integral.
He states:
- (1) the d'Alembert/Lagrange form Σ ä δa + δG = 0, for all δa, δb, δc with δ(abc) = 0, i.e. δc/c = −δa/a − δb/b (written at the bottom of the page);
- (2) the energy integral ½(ȧ² + ḃ² + ċ²) + G = const. Here G is the part of the vis viva not due to the change of shape, i.e. reduced (effective) potential plus the rotational kinetic terms.

Equilibria. Constant form (ȧ = ḃ = ċ = 0) holds if and only if the first variation of G vanishes subject to abc = const, i.e. a ∂G/∂a = b ∂G/∂b = c ∂G/∂c. This reproduces the equilibrium equations (3) or (4), (5) of the memoir. The equilibrium is labile if G is not a minimum, since then infinitely small disturbances can produce a complete change of the state.

Substituting τ², τ'² from (3) gives G a value (left blank on the page) that is always negative at a stationary point.

Existence of a stable figure: K → 0 when one axis becomes infinitely small or infinitely large under abc = const. K is greatest for the sphere of radius ∛(a₀b₀c₀). Hence G tends to a non-negative limit at the boundary and can never become negatively infinite. So G attains a (negative) minimum, which is a stable steady figure.
errors: Eq. (1) as transcribed has first derivatives ∂a/∂t; for consistency with the energy integral (2) these must be second derivatives ∂²a/∂t² (as in the printed memoir). This is either a slip in the draft or a misreading.

The claim that a minimum of G implies stability is only a sufficient criterion, and only for perturbations within the class of ellipsoidal motions about a principal axis. Riemann went further in the memoir and asserted instability whenever G is not a minimum. Lebovitz (1966) and Chandrasekhar (EFE, 1969) showed his stability conclusions for the Riemann ellipsoids are partly incorrect, because secular (energy) and ordinary (dynamical) stability differ.
The intermediate value of G after substitution is left blank, and the passage about the sign (≷ 2πε²) is heavily struck out and fragmentary. The boundary argument is only sketched.

results.what: A liquid ellipsoid preserving its shape must have its rotation axis and angular-momentum normal in a principal plane. The motion is a rigid rotation plus internal motion along similar ellipses perpendicular to that plane.
results.modern_name: Riemann ellipsoids (Riemann's theorem on self-gravitating ellipsoids, types S, I, II, III)

results.what: Reduction of the axis dynamics, for rotation about a principal axis, to a point mass on abc = const with potential G = τ²/(a−b)² + τ'²/(a+b)² − 2εK, plus the energy integral.
results.modern_name: Lagrangian/Hamiltonian reduction of Dirichlet–Dedekind–Riemann ellipsoid dynamics; effective potential

results.what: Equilibria are stationary points of G under abc = const. Stability holds where G is a minimum. Existence of a minimum follows because G is bounded below with non-negative boundary limits.
results.modern_name: Energy (variational, secular) stability criterion for Riemann/Jacobi/Dedekind ellipsoids
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1861 (criticized and corrected by Lebovitz 1966 and Chandrasekhar 1969)

results.what: The constraint abc = const gives δc/c = −δa/a − δb/b.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of material printed in Riemann's 1861 ellipsoid memoir (shape-preservation theorem, point-mass/potential reformulation, energy stability criterion). These results are well known as his. Only draft-level variants appear.

checkable.asserts: δc/c = −δa/a − δb/b preserves abc to first order.
For the sphere, K = ∫_0^∞ ds/(r²+s)^{3/2} = 2/r, its maximal value at fixed abc = r³.

checkable.asserts: With the second-derivative form of (1) and a Lagrange multiplier, dE/dt = λ·d(abc)/dt, which vanishes on abc = const. This is the energy integral (2).
